💻 Pocketbyte: Modular Computer the Size of a Card

Pocketbyte is a tiny portable computer measuring about 75 × 55 mm, roughly the size of a credit card. It runs on an ESP32-S3 processor with 8 MB PSRAM, has a 2.8-inch IPS screen, 1500 mAh battery, microSD slot for up to 32 GB, a mono speaker, and a 3.5 mm jack.

Its key feature is a modular pin connector that lets you attach hardware like a gamepad for retro emulators, a BlackBerry-style QWERTY keyboard, or a development board to control other electronics. The software is open source, based on FreeRTOS, supports Arduino, and apps can be installed via Wi-Fi from a built-in store.

❗️15 U.S. attorneys general are turning up the heat on OpenAI

The fallout from OpenAI’s recent AI security incidents isn’t over yet.

A coalition of 15 state attorneys general has formally ordered the company to preserve a huge range of evidence tied to the Hugging Face breach and earlier containment failures. That includes internal chats, model logs, safety procedures, technical documents, and other records that could become crucial if legal action follows.

The coalition is also demanding that OpenAI pause any evaluations that encourage AI models to explore advanced cyberattack techniques until the company can prove those systems are securely contained.

They’re also calling for stronger protections for whistleblowers, saying employees who report dangerous or unlawful behavior should be protected from retaliation.

Perhaps most notably, regulators want OpenAI to preserve evidence related to earlier reports of unauthorized network access, exposed credentials, and claims that one AI agent left “escape instructions” for future versions of itself.

The attorneys general say these incidents may have violated consumer-protection and data-privacy laws. No lawsuit has been filed yet, but an evidence-preservation order is often the first sign that regulators are preparing for a potentially major legal battle.

⚠️ OpenAI fires back in Apple’s trade secrets lawsuit

After Apple accused OpenAI of stealing confidential hardware secrets through former engineer Chang Liu, OpenAI released internal messages that appear to show Apple employees continuing to rely on Liu weeks after he had already left the company.

According to the messages, Apple employees asked Liu to locate internal files, explain product design decisions, and answer technical questions. One employee even wrote:

“Of course, I could ask several folks, but you are the best. Even if you don’t work here anymore.”

OpenAI also claims Apple made another embarrassing mistake. Apple alleged it reached out to OpenAI before filing the lawsuit and received no response. But emails released by OpenAI suggest Apple’s outside lawyer accidentally thanked OpenAI’s General Counsel for a phone call that never actually happened before later apologizing for the mix-up.

That said, these revelations don’t disprove Apple’s core allegations that trade secrets were taken. Instead, they shift some attention back to Apple, raising uncomfortable questions about its own security practices.

If Apple believed Liu had access to highly sensitive information, why were employees still asking him for confidential help after he had already left the company? 🤔
